name: The Dayan
line: A commander who strikes first and overturns the board
story: The preemptive strike of the Six-Day War (1967)
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Independent and Speed, this type believes that the actual strength of armies, more than diplomatic notes or treaties, decides outcomes, and trusts a result won by defeating the other side more than a peace bought with concessions. It acts on its own judgment rather than waiting for allies to agree, and it chooses to strike before the other side has finished gathering its forces. Convinced that a long war lets outside pressure in, it tries to settle matters within days. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to the leader who picks a no-warning air strike on Monday morning over a blockade, and who lets not a single ship through the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba).

figure.name: Moshe Dayan
figure.life: Born on 20 May 1915 at Kibbutz Degania Alef in Palestine, he grew up in the Haganah, the Jewish self-defense organization. On 8 June 1941, in Lebanon, a sniper’s bullet cost him his left eye, and the black eye patch became his emblem. He became chief of staff in December 1953 and commanded the Sinai campaign of 1956; on 1 June 1967 he became defense minister and led Israel through the Six-Day War. But he failed to forestall the surprise attack that opened the Yom Kippur War in 1973 and was called to account for the lack of preparedness. Although the Agranat Commission, on 1 April 1974, did not assign him ministerial responsibility, he left office along with Meir’s cabinet amid public condemnation. As foreign minister in Begin’s government from 1977, he took part in the Camp David Accords of 1978. He is criticized for breaking the law by using soldiers to dig up antiquities, which he also traded. He died of a heart attack on 16 October 1981 and was buried at Nahalal, the village where he grew up.
figure.story: After Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping on 22–23 May 1967, Israel formed a government of national unity on 1 June with Dayan as defense minister, and on 4 June it decided on war. At 7:45 on the morning of 5 June the Israeli air force sent up all but 12 of its roughly 200 operational aircraft and struck 11 Egyptian airfields. The first wave destroyed 197 Egyptian aircraft on the ground; by about noon some 450 Egyptian, Jordanian and Syrian aircraft had been wiped out, for the loss of 19 Israeli planes. Ground forces took Sinai and Gaza, the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights, and the fighting ended on 10 June.

kin.name: Ariel Sharon
kin.why: In the Yom Kippur War of 1973 he took his armored division across the Suez Canal against the wishes of his superiors and encircled the Egyptian Third Army. But as defense minister in 1982 he drove the Lebanon war beyond the line the cabinet had approved, and the Kahan Commission found that he bore personal responsibility for the Sabra and Shatila massacre.

kin.name: Yamamoto Isoroku
kin.why: He opposed war with the United States, but once war was decided he struck the US Pacific Fleet first, in the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 (Hawaii time). He lost four aircraft carriers at Midway in June 1942, and on 18 April 1943 he was shot down and killed over Bougainville.

you: Time and again you judged that you had to move before the other side finished its preparations. What you dislike most is missing a chance while waiting for someone else’s permission, and your aim is to secure a clear result in a short time. By the same token, you tend to shoulder the consequences of your decisions yourself rather than pass them on to others.
caution: After one great victory it is easy to discount the chance that the other side will strike first next time. On the morning of 6 October 1973 Dayan opposed the full mobilization his chief of staff demanded; at 2 p.m. that afternoon Egypt and Syria attacked by surprise, and Israel lost more than 2,500 dead.

name: The Giap
line: A patient guardian who yields ground but never submits
story: Dien Bien Phu (1954) and the long war
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Independent and Caution, this type believes that strength decides the contest in the end and does not bow to the other side’s demands, but it never stakes all its strength on a single decisive battle. Rather than wait for help from others, it holds out with its own land and its own army, delaying the decision until time and distance wear the enemy down. If it judges itself not ready, it will put off even an attack date already set, and it asks first what must be kept to the very end before counting what it loses today. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to the side that keeps work on the missiles going while holding its ships short of the blockade line, waiting for the other side to tire first.

figure.name: Võ Nguyên Giáp
figure.life: Born on 25 August 1911 in Quảng Bình province in French Indochina, he studied law in Hanoi but never became a lawyer, and taught history at the Thăng Long school. His first wife, Nguyễn Thị Quang Thái, was arrested by the French colonial authorities and died in Hanoi’s Hỏa Lò prison. In December 1944 he formed the first armed propaganda unit, the starting point of the Vietnam People’s Army, and in 1954 he defeated the French at Dien Bien Phu. In the war against the United States he is said to have opposed the Tet Offensive of 1968, and after the spring offensive of 1972 failed with heavy losses he handed field command to Văn Tiến Dũng. He remained defense minister until 1980 and left the Politburo in 1982. Critics call him a commander who spent far too many lives; admirers say he lost many battles yet won the war. He died in a military hospital in Hanoi on 4 October 2013, at 102, and was buried in his native Quảng Bình.
figure.story: When French troops parachuted into the valley of Dien Bien Phu on 20 November 1953 and built a fortress there, Giáp decided to open a Chinese-style “swift attack, swift victory” assault on 25 January 1954, put it off a day to the 26th, then canceled it altogether. He switched to a siege, digging his guns into the forward slopes of the hills and ringing the fortress with trenches, and he later called this the hardest decision of his military life. The attack that began on 13 March went on for 54 days; on 7 May the French garrison surrendered, and 11,721 men were taken prisoner. The very next day, 8 May, the Geneva Conference took up the question of Indochina, and under the accords reached that July, Vietnam was divided in two at the 17th parallel.

kin.name: Mao Zedong
kin.why: On the Long March that began in October 1934 he endured losses so heavy that of about 100,000 people only 7,000–8,000 reached Shaanxi, and in Yan’an he set out his theory of protracted war, which wears the enemy down. He founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, but by some estimates tens of millions died in the famine of the Great Leap Forward, and he bears heavy responsibility for the Cultural Revolution as well.

kin.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus
kin.why: Made dictator after the defeat at Lake Trasimene in 217 BC, he avoided a decisive battle with Hannibal and pursued a strategy of delay, cutting off his supplies. The Romans at first mocked him as “the Delayer,” but after the commanders who chose a pitched battle at Cannae in 216 BC were crushed, they followed his way again.

you: You have chosen not to kneel to the other side’s terms, even at a cost. You value the strength that will still be there at the end more than face or a single piece of ground today, and you are used to waiting until a hurried opponent wears himself out. You also know that this approach works only if you can endure the pressure and blame of those around you for a long time.
caution: It is easy to make light of the price paid while holding out. Even at Dien Bien Phu, which Giáp won, Viet Minh deaths came to about 8,000 by French estimates and to 4,020 even by the Vietnamese government’s count, and the spring offensive of 1972 failed at heavy cost, after which he gave up field command.

name: The MacArthur
line: A commander who leads allied armies and stakes all on the decisive battle
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Alliance and Speed, this type believes problems must be settled by force, but rather than fight alone it pools the armies and resources of its allies. It takes on the work of moving the forces of many nations under a single plan, yet it draws up the frame of that plan itself and pushes it through by winning over the staff officers who object. When it sees the other side stretched thin, it tries to turn the tide with one great operation. Among the leaders of October 1962, it comes closest to one who, as soon as the OAS resolution is passed and NATO has been informed, sets the air strike and invasion plans in motion.

figure.name: Douglas MacArthur
figure.life: The son of a soldier, he was born on 26 January 1880 in the barracks at Little Rock, Arkansas, and graduated first in his class from the US Military Academy at West Point in 1903. In the First World War he fought as chief of staff of the 42nd Division and as a brigade commander. As Army chief of staff from 1930 to 1935, he drew criticism in 1932 for using troops to break up the veterans’ protest in Washington. After leaving Corregidor in the Philippines for Australia in March 1942, he declared, “I shall return.” From August 1945 he directed the occupation of Japan as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, and in July 1950 he became commander of the UN forces, turning the tide with the Inchon landing before being driven back hard after China intervened. He clashed with President Truman by pressing to widen the war and was dismissed on 11 April 1951; some see the dismissal as the natural working of civilian control, others as a blow to national pride. He died in Washington on 5 April 1964.
figure.story: At a conference in Tokyo on 23 August 1950, naval officers objected to Inchon, citing its narrow channel, swift currents and average tidal range of 8.8 meters, and recommended Kunsan instead. MacArthur held out for Inchon, arguing that only a blow where the North Koreans did not expect it would cut their supply lines, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff approved on 28 August. At 6:30 on the morning of 15 September Marines landed on Wolmi-do and held the island by noon, and the main force came ashore on the evening tide. The operation involved 261 ships and about 75,000 men from eight nations: the United States, South Korea, Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, France and the Netherlands. On 16 September the Eighth Army on the Pusan Perimeter went over to the counterattack, and on 28 September the North Koreans were driven out of Seoul.

kin.name: Norman Schwarzkopf
kin.why: In command of a multinational force of about 500,000 American troops and about 250,000 from other countries, he opened the air campaign on 17 January 1991, began the ground war on 24 February and drove the Iraqi army out of Kuwait in about 100 hours. He is also criticized, however, because the ceasefire terms allowed Iraq to fly armed helicopters, which were then used to crush uprisings.

kin.name: Ferdinand Foch
kin.why: At the Doullens conference on 26 March 1918 he was given the coordination of Allied operations and went on to become supreme commander. After halting the German offensive that July, he ended the war with the Hundred Days Offensive and received the German request for an armistice at Compiègne on 11 November. His doctrine of the offensive, which cost enormous numbers of lives in the Artois offensives of 1915 and elsewhere, has drawn criticism.

you: You judged that winning together is surer than winning alone. You do not shirk the labor of aligning plans with allies, but once the preparations are done you do not put off the decision; you take the big step. And if things go badly, you are ready to take the responsibility yourself.
caution: Confidence after a great victory makes it easy to underrate the chance that someone else will intervene. On Wake Island on 15 October 1950 MacArthur told Truman there was very little chance China would come in; on 24 November he pushed north toward the Yalu, met a massive Chinese offensive the next day, and by the end of December had been driven out of North Korea.

name: The Ben-Gurion
line: A founder who holds out while drawing in allies and arms
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Alliance and Caution, this type believes force must be met with force when the other side pushes, and refuses a peace bought by compromising on bad terms. Yet it also knows it cannot win alone, so while it holds out it works hard to win recognition and arms from the great powers. Rather than rush to a decision, it uses even a ceasefire as time to build up its army, and it thinks first about enduring for a long time without collapsing. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to Macmillan’s stance on 27 October: keep the blockade in place, gather the allies’ support, and accept that no one can escape his own danger with a deal that sacrifices an ally.

figure.name: David Ben-Gurion
figure.life: Born on 16 October 1886 in Płońsk, in Russian Poland, he landed at Jaffa in Palestine in September 1906. As secretary-general of the Histadrut labor federation from 1921 to 1935 and chairman of the Jewish Agency Executive from 1935 to 1948, he became the effective leader of the Jewish community. On 14 May 1948 he proclaimed independence in Tel Aviv and became the first prime minister and defense minister, leading the country until 1953 and again from 1955 to 1963. In 1948 he ordered the Irgun’s arms ship Altalena taken by force, and 19 people died; in 1953 he denied that the army had been involved in the Qibya massacre. The historian Benny Morris judges that, although there was no explicit order to expel the Arab inhabitants in 1948, a climate accepting expulsion took shape under his leadership. He died on 1 December 1973 and was buried near Sde Boker.
figure.story: On 12 May 1948 the People’s Administration rejected an American truce proposal and voted 6 to 4 for a declaration of independence, and at 4 p.m. on 14 May Ben-Gurion proclaimed independence in Tel Aviv. Eleven minutes after the declaration took effect at midnight, the United States recognized the new state; the Soviet Union followed on 17 May. When the armies of five Arab states came in on 15 May, Israel’s forces numbered 29,677, but by putting Czechoslovak arms and the first truce, from 11 June to 8 July, to work building up the army, Israel had 108,300 under arms by 30 December. In 1949 it signed armistice agreements, from Egypt on 24 February to Syria on 20 July, and held about 78% of Mandatory Palestine, but 6,373 Israelis had lost their lives.

kin.name: Konrad Adenauer
kin.why: Becoming West Germany’s first chancellor in 1949, he rejected Stalin’s offer of a united, neutral Germany in 1952 and chose to bind the country to the West, achieving rearmament through NATO membership in May 1955 and the founding of the Bundeswehr that November. He was criticized for keeping at his side Globke, who had helped draft racial laws under the Nazis.

kin.name: Winston Churchill
kin.why: Becoming prime minister in 1940, he rejected any compromise with Germany even after France fell, and held out through the Battle of Britain from July to October that year. Meanwhile, on 2 September, he obtained 50 American destroyers in exchange for leases on bases, and on 11 March 1941 he drew in American aid through Lend-Lease. He was voted out of office in the general election of July 1945.

you: Even when the odds were against you, you chose to hold out rather than accept the other side’s terms. You admit that you cannot solve everything on your own strength, and aim instead to buy time until you can draw in nations that will fight beside you. Nor do you take lightly the power of words and symbols to keep up people’s morale.
caution: It is easy to overrate the strength of the great powers you have joined hands with. At Sèvres in October 1956 Ben-Gurion made a secret agreement with Britain and France and invaded Sinai on 29 October, but under pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the UN he withdrew in March 1957, and it became plain that Britain and France could not act without the United States.

name: The Nasser
line: A gambler who seizes first and makes it stick through diplomacy
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Independent and Speed, this type moves first when the chance comes, takes what can be had, and is skilled at locking in the result through diplomacy and negotiation afterward. It trusts strength but does not cling to a fight to the finish, and it plays on the rivalry of the great powers to get what it needs without being bound to either. Its decisions are quick and its calculations clear, but by the same token it risks provoking its opponent and its neighbors all at once. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to Khrushchev’s letter of 27 October, which sought to trade missiles already in place for a pledge of no invasion and the bases in Turkey.

figure.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
figure.life: Born in Alexandria on 15 January 1918, the son of a post office clerk, he became an army officer, and in the first Arab–Israeli war of 1948 he fought as deputy commander of a unit besieged at Falluja. In July 1952 he led the Free Officers in overthrowing the monarchy, and after a member of the Muslim Brotherhood tried to assassinate him in October 1954 he launched a crackdown in which thousands were arrested. He became president in June 1956 and nationalized the Suez Canal that year; the United Arab Republic he formed with Syria in 1958 broke apart in 1961. When defeat by Israel in June 1967 cost Egypt the Sinai Peninsula, he announced his resignation on 9 June, then withdrew it at the crowds’ demand. He is hailed as the symbol of Arab nationalism and condemned as an authoritarian who banned political parties in 1953 and then crushed opponents through one-party and military rule. He died of a heart attack in Cairo on 28 September 1970, and more than five million people are said to have turned out for his funeral.
figure.story: When the United States withdrew its promise to help finance the Aswan High Dam on 19 July 1956, Nasser declared in a speech in Alexandria on 26 July that he was nationalizing the Suez Canal Company, owned by British and French capital, and said the shareholders would be compensated. Britain and France secretly joined hands with Israel: on 29 October the Israeli army advanced into Sinai, and on 31 October British and French aircraft bombed Egyptian airfields. But under pressure from the United States and the UN a ceasefire took hold on 6–7 November. British and French troops left before the year was out, and the Israelis withdrew in March 1957. Egypt kept the canal, and it paid the canal company compensation in installments, completing payment in 1962.

kin.name: Indira Gandhi
kin.why: After concluding a treaty with the Soviet Union in August 1971, she seized on Pakistan’s air strikes of 3 December to send troops into East Pakistan, and on 16 December in Dhaka she took the surrender of about 93,000 Pakistani troops. Under the Simla Agreement of 2 July the following year she handed back most of the occupied territory in return for a promise that disputes would be dealt with only between the two countries.

kin.name: Sukarno
kin.why: Confronting the Netherlands over West New Guinea, he bought Soviet arms, ordered a military operation on 19 December 1961 and sent in paratroopers in 1962. When the United States stepped in to mediate, he signed the New York Agreement on 15 August 1962 and called off a full invasion; after a period of temporary UN administration, the territory passed to Indonesia on 1 May 1963.

you: You chose to move without hesitation when you saw an opening, but to leave the keeping of your gains to negotiation. You value the results actually left in your hands more than principle, and you think alliances and promises, too, can be recalculated for the sake of those results. Your judgment is quick and your sense of gain and loss is clear, but you need to factor in how others will remember you.
caution: Repeat a first move that worked once, and the other side may strike first. In May 1967 Nasser sent a large army into Sinai, had the UN force withdrawn, and on 22–23 May closed the Straits of Tiran; on 5 June Israel struck first, and within days he had lost the whole of the Sinai Peninsula.

name: The Tito
line: A pragmatist who walks the tightrope between great powers
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Independent and Caution, this type holds that a country must have the strength to defend itself, yet rather than collide head-on with the great powers it sets them to check one another and draws practical gains from the space between them. It entrusts itself to neither camp, accepting help from both while letting neither push it around. It does not hurry, watching the other side’s moves and searching patiently for ways to cut its losses. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to the position of the non-aligned nations, which sided with neither superpower and called for the blockade and the arms shipments to be halted together.

figure.name: Josip Broz Tito
figure.life: He was born on 7 May 1892 in Kumrovec, in the Croatian lands of Austria-Hungary, to a Croat father and a Slovene mother. In the First World War he was taken prisoner by the Russians in March 1915; he became a communist in revolutionary Russia and returned home, was sentenced to five years in 1928, and from 1937 led the Communist Party. In the Second World War he commanded the Partisans against the German and Italian occupiers; after the war he took power, and from 1974 he ruled as president for life until his death in Ljubljana on 4 May 1980. He is praised as a leader who held to an independent course against the Soviet Union and championed workers’ self-management, and condemned as a dictator who jailed opponents under one-party rule and from 1949 interned people branded pro-Soviet on the island of Goli Otok and elsewhere. At his funeral in Belgrade on 8 May, 128 of the UN’s 154 member states were represented.
figure.story: When Stalin had the Communist Party of Yugoslavia expelled through the Cominform resolution published on 28 June 1948, Tito did not give in, and when the Soviet bloc closed its borders to squeeze him, he asked the United States for help that summer. The United States decided on economic aid in February 1949 and added Yugoslavia to its military aid program in 1951; in February 1953 Tito concluded the Balkan Pact with Greece and Turkey, yet he stayed out of NATO. After Stalin’s death, Khrushchev came to Belgrade in 1955 and on 2 June signed a declaration pledging non-interference in Yugoslavia’s internal affairs. On 19 July 1956 Tito issued a joint declaration with Nehru and Nasser on the island of Brioni, and from 1 to 6 September 1961 he hosted the first Non-Aligned summit in Belgrade.

kin.name: Norodom Sihanouk
kin.why: After winning independence from France in November 1953, he proclaimed neutrality and walked a tightrope between the United States and the communist bloc. He refused American aid in November 1963 and broke off relations with the United States in May 1965, while secretly allowing North Vietnam passage through Cambodian territory; on 18 March 1970, while he was abroad, Lon Nol’s faction deposed him.

kin.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
kin.why: As independent India’s first prime minister he championed non-alignment; in 1955 he set up the Bhilai steelworks with Soviet help while also accepting Western aid. When India was driven back in the border war with China in October–November 1962, he asked Kennedy for fighter aircraft on 19 November; when he needed to, he reached out to either side.

you: Even facing a strong opponent, you did not hurry to take sides. You weigh what your country can actually gain and keep before causes or camps, and you aim for a position in which you are no one’s pawn yet obtain what you need from several sides. You know well that holding such a position takes constant calculation and patience.
caution: When the gains of the tightrope rest on one man’s skill, no one can take them over once he is gone. After Tito’s death in 1980, Yugoslavia, governed under the 1974 constitution by a collective presidency that rotated every year, lost its center, and starting with the declarations of independence by Slovenia and Croatia on 25 June 1991, it broke apart in war.

name: The Nixon
line: A pragmatist who deals even with enemies to change the board fast
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Alliance and Speed, this type believes the balance of power decides outcomes, but rather than use force directly it prefers to create new relationships quickly through deals. It will join hands even with yesterday’s enemy when interests meet, and, unbound by form and procedure, it uses secret contacts if need be to decide before the chance slips away. It also works hard to win over public opinion by putting principle and interest forward together. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to the side that builds a quick way out through a deal even if that means going around procedure, like the private understanding Robert Kennedy offered Dobrynin on the night of 27 October.

figure.name: Richard Nixon
figure.life: Born on 9 January 1913 into a Quaker family in Yorba Linda, California, he graduated from Duke University’s law school. Elected to the House in 1946, he made his name as an anticommunist in the Alger Hiss case, then became a senator in 1950 and Eisenhower’s vice president from 1953 to 1961. He lost narrowly to Kennedy in the presidential election of 1960 and was beaten again in the 1962 race for governor of California, but he won the presidency in 1968. While pulling American troops out of Vietnam, he announced the invasion of Cambodia in April 1970 and met fierce opposition. He is remembered as the diplomat who changed the shape of the Cold War with his visit to China and the strategic arms limitation agreement with the Soviet Union in 1972, and also as the only American president to resign, on 9 August 1974, over the cover-up of the Watergate affair. President Ford pardoned him on 8 September that year, and he died in New York on 22 April 1994.
figure.story: Taking as his signal China’s invitation to the American table tennis team in April 1971, and Zhou Enlai’s reception of the players on 14 April, Nixon sent Kissinger secretly to Beijing by way of Pakistan in July. On 15 July Nixon astonished the world by announcing on television that he had accepted Zhou’s invitation to visit China, and from 21 to 28 February 1972 he became the first American president to visit China, meeting Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai. In the Shanghai Communiqué of 27 February the two countries agreed to work toward normal relations and set the question of Taiwan aside. The deal gave the United States a lever against the Soviet Union, reopened contacts broken off for 23 years, and led to diplomatic relations in 1979.

kin.name: Zhou Enlai
kin.why: China’s premier from 1949 until his death, he represented his country at the Geneva Conference of 1954 and the Bandung Conference of 1955. He opened contacts by receiving the American table tennis team on 14 April 1971, and after receiving Kissinger’s secret visit that July he prepared Nixon’s visit of 1972. He is also criticized for going along with Mao during the Cultural Revolution.

kin.name: Ronald Reagan
kin.why: A president who had taken a hard line on the Soviet Union, he met Gorbachev for the first time in Geneva in November 1985 and opened the way to bargaining; after Reykjavik in October 1986, he signed the INF Treaty in Washington on 8 December 1987, eliminating all ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500–5,500 km. In May 1988 he visited Moscow.

you: You were quick to reach out first rather than miss a chance. You value ways of getting things done over purity of principle, and you aim to find quickly where interests meet and build an alliance there. When procedure slows things down, you have no qualms about finding another way around it.
caution: Join hands quickly with a new partner through a secret deal, and you easily lose the trust of old allies. When Nixon announced his plan to visit China on 15 July 1971, he had not told allies such as Japan and South Korea in advance, and the news came as a great shock; Taiwan saw it as betrayal and lodged a formal protest.

name: The Kissinger
line: An alliance architect who designs the balance of power
story: Détente and the balance of power (1969–1977)
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Alliance and Caution, this type sees power as the foundation of international relations, but uses it to weave a balance among many states rather than to wage war. It believes it can deal even with hostile states, and it sets adversaries to check one another so that no single state can overturn the order on its own. Its aim is to avoid a great war, and it moves carefully, one step at a time, through secret contacts and agreements reached in stages. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to the idea, floated on 22 October, of withdrawing missiles from non-nuclear countries in a single package, taking the missiles out of Cuba, Turkey and Italy together so that both sides had room to step back.

figure.name: Henry Kissinger
figure.life: Born on 27 May 1923 into a Jewish family in Fürth, Germany, he fled Nazi persecution to New York in 1938, served in the US Army in the Second World War, and went on to become a professor at Harvard. As national security adviser to Nixon and Ford from 1969 to 1975 and secretary of state from 1973 to 1977, he led détente with the Soviet Union, the opening to China and the Vietnam peace negotiations. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Le Duc Tho for the Paris Accords of 1973, though Le Duc Tho declined it, and by shuttling between Egypt and Israel he also secured agreements to disengage their forces in Sinai. He is praised as a master of realist diplomacy who helped avoid nuclear war through the balance of power, and accused of war crimes by critics who hold him responsible for civilian deaths through the bombing of Cambodia, involvement in the coup in Chile and more. In 1982 he founded the consulting firm Kissinger Associates, which he ran into his last years, and he died at Kent, Connecticut, on 29 November 2023, at 100.
figure.story: Setting out on an Asian tour on 1 July 1971, Kissinger feigned illness in Islamabad, Pakistan, and was given out to be resting at a hill resort; at noon on 9 July he landed in Beijing aboard a Pakistani aircraft for two days of talks with China’s leaders. When Nixon announced the trip and his own plan to visit China on 15 July, the Soviet Union too hurried to negotiate with the United States, and after visiting Beijing in February 1972, Nixon signed the strategic arms limitation agreement and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with Brezhnev in Moscow on 26 May. This arrangement, which placed the United States at the center of the balance by dealing separately with two communist giants that had fallen out, was called “triangular diplomacy” and became the framework of détente.

kin.name: Klemens von Metternich
kin.why: As Austria’s foreign minister from 1809 to 1848, he led the Congress of Vienna in 1814–1815, designing the balance among Europe’s great powers after the Napoleonic Wars, and upheld that order for thirty years. He suppressed liberal and nationalist movements with the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819, and the revolution of 1848 drove him from office and into exile.

kin.name: James Baker
kin.why: As US secretary of state from 1989 to 1992, after Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990 he traveled the world for nearly ten weeks, assembling a coalition of about 42 nations and securing UN Security Council Resolution 678 on 29 November. In 1991 he convened the Madrid Conference, bringing Israel and the Arab side to the same table.

you: You cared more about building a structure in which the other side would not come at you again than about defeating it. You do not fix friends and enemies in place but adjust relations as needed, aiming for an order in which your country’s position endures without a great war. You tend to picture the situation a few years ahead before thinking of the victory in front of you.
caution: Put the balance among great powers first, and it is easy to push the fate of small allies aside. After Kissinger won the withdrawal of US troops with the Paris Accords of 27 January 1973, the agreement soon broke down, and South Vietnam ceased to exist when Saigon fell on 30 April 1975.

name: The de Gaulle
line: A man of principle who raises the flag alone
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Independent and Speed, this type believes that legitimacy and principle, more than force, win in the end, and it accepts no compromise that violates principle. It does not wait for others to decide; it states its position clearly and first, alone if necessary, and rallies people to it. It insists on equal standing even with allies, putting its country’s prestige first even when it is the one receiving help. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to Castro’s stance on 30 October, when he turned away UN inspectors on the ground that inspection could be imposed only on a conquered country.

figure.name: Charles de Gaulle
figure.life: Born in Lille on 22 November 1890, he became a professional soldier. When France fell to Germany in June 1940 he founded Free France in London and led the resistance, and after the liberation of Paris in 1944 he headed the provisional government until he stepped down in 1946. Recalled amid the Algerian crisis of 1958, he became prime minister on 1 June, and on 21 December that year he was elected president, opening the Fifth Republic. France carried out its first nuclear test in the Sahara on 13 February 1960; the Évian Accords of March 1962 ended the Algerian War, and in January 1964 France established diplomatic relations with China. His independent course, owing nothing to the United States, is praised for restoring France’s autonomy and criticized for concentrating power in his own hands and shaking the alliance. He rode out the protests of May 1968, but after losing a referendum in April 1969 he resigned the next day, and he died at his home in Colombey-les-Deux-Églises on 9 November 1970.
figure.story: At a press conference on 21 February 1966, de Gaulle announced that French forces would be withdrawn from NATO command and that foreign forces on French soil could stay only under French command. On 7 March he formally notified the allies, and in a letter to President Johnson on 9 March he announced that France would recover full sovereignty over its territory and end its part in the integrated military command. On 1 July the French forces in West Germany left NATO command; by 1 April 1967 some 26,000 American and Canadian troops, and their bases, had to leave France, and Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe moved out of Paris as well. France nonetheless remained a party to the North Atlantic Treaty itself.

kin.name: Syngman Rhee
kin.why: As the first president of the Republic of Korea, on 18 June 1953 he ordered the release of anticommunist prisoners of war without consulting the United States, shaking the armistice talks, and he never signed the armistice of 27 July. Some see this decision, which pitted him head-on against an ally while he depended on its aid, as independent diplomacy; others call it reckless.

kin.name: Olof Palme
kin.why: As prime minister, in a radio address on 23 December 1972 he condemned the American bombing of Hanoi, comparing it to Guernica, Treblinka and other atrocities, and the United States froze diplomatic relations for more than a year. Holding to a course that lined up behind neither superpower, he was assassinated on a Stockholm street on 28 February 1986.

you: Even when the odds were against you, you chose to put principle first and proclaim it openly, alone if need be. You consider it more important to make clear the legitimacy your country must uphold than to shift position to suit other nations' calculations. Even when receiving help you want to be treated as an equal, and you accept that this will often bring you into conflict with your partners.
caution: Stubbornness in defense of prestige easily spills over into friction with allies. When de Gaulle cried “Vive le Québec libre!” from the balcony of Montreal’s city hall on 24 July 1967, Canada’s prime minister, Pearson, declared the remark unacceptable, and de Gaulle cut his visit short and went home.

name: The King
line: A resister who held to the principle of nonviolence to the end
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Independent and Caution, this type refuses to overpower the other side by force and makes fidelity to a principle it believes right its strongest instrument. It will not yield an inch on principle, but instead of violence or surprise it chooses pressure and persuasion sustained over a long time. Rather than borrow others' strength, it sets an example itself so that people follow. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to U Thant’s stance on 24 October, when he appealed to both sides for restraint, saying that his concern was not the legality of the blockade but only averting the crisis.

figure.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
figure.life: Born in Atlanta on 15 January 1929, the son of a Baptist minister, he became a minister himself. Leading the Montgomery bus boycott, which began on 5 December 1955, made him known across the country, and in January 1957 he founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) and became its president. The letter he wrote in jail after his arrest in Birmingham in April 1963, and the March on Washington that August, made him the symbol of the movement, and on 10 December 1964 he received the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo. In 1965 he led the march from Selma to Montgomery, helping to win the Voting Rights Act; in 1966 he moved to Chicago to take on discrimination in the North, and there he was attacked by white mobs. When he came out publicly against the Vietnam War in 1967, criticism poured in from the press and from inside and outside the movement, and pressure from the FBI intensified. On 4 April 1968, in Memphis to support a strike by sanitation workers, he was shot dead on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel.
figure.story: On 28 August 1963 more than 250,000 people gathered for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Conceived by the labor leader A. Philip Randolph and organized by Bayard Rustin, the march demanded a federal jobs program, a higher minimum wage, passage of a civil rights bill, the integration of public schools and a ban on discrimination in employment. King spoke last, in front of the Lincoln Memorial, and partway through he set aside his prepared text and said, “I have a dream.” The civil rights legislation President Kennedy had proposed that June, carried forward by the pressure the march brought to bear, was enacted as the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

kin.name: Václav Havel
kin.why: A playwright who urged “living in truth” under the communist regime, he led the human rights declaration Charter 77 in 1977 and then spent years in prison for his dissident activity. In 1989 he led the Velvet Revolution, changing the regime without violence, and became president.

kin.name: Andrei Sakharov
kin.why: A key physicist in the Soviet hydrogen bomb program, he set himself against the system in 1968 with an essay published in the West that called for nuclear arms reduction and an end to the persecution of dissidents. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975 but barred from leaving the country, and in 1980 he was exiled to Gorky, returning to Moscow only in 1986.

you: You cared as much about how you win as about winning. Even when an easy shortcut was there, you did not take it if it went against principle, choosing instead, however long it took, the path by which the other side loses its own legitimacy. What you aim for is not a result won by force but one that people accept as right.
caution: A decision to keep faith with principle can drive away those who stood beside you. When King condemned the Vietnam War at Riverside Church in New York on 4 April 1967, the Washington Post wrote that he had diminished his usefulness to his own cause, and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) criticized him for tying together two unrelated issues.

name: The Truman
line: An enforcer who steps in the moment the rules are broken
story: The Berlin Airlift (1948) and entry into the Korean War (1950)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Alliance and Speed, this type holds that a breach of the rules of international order must not be left to stand, and it responds with action, not words alone. Rather than step forward alone, it acts in the name of international organizations or allies to give its response legitimacy. It does not drag out decisions, and it makes plain that it will carry their weight itself. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to the decisions of 23 October: proclaim the quarantine on the strength of the OAS resolution, and if a reconnaissance plane is shot down, strike the surface-to-air missile sites at once.

figure.name: Harry S. Truman
figure.life: Born in Lamar, Missouri, on 8 May 1884, he never finished college, and in the First World War he fought in France as an artillery captain. When his men’s clothing store failed in 1922 he was left deep in debt; he went into local politics and was elected to the Senate in 1934. Sworn in as vice president on 20 January 1945, he became president on 12 April, 82 days later, when Roosevelt died. That August he approved the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, which some credit with ending the war sooner and others condemn as the mass killing of civilians. With the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin Airlift and the founding of NATO he set the frame of US foreign policy in the early Cold War, and he won reelection over Dewey in 1948. In 1950 he decided to enter the Korean War, and after he dismissed MacArthur in April 1951 his approval ratings fell sharply. He left office in 1953 and died in Kansas City on 26 December 1972.
figure.story: When the Soviet Union declared on 24 June 1948 that four-power administration of Berlin was at an end and cut the routes into West Berlin, the United States and Britain began flying in food and fuel on 26 June. On 28 June, when the question of whether to stay in Berlin came up, Truman said flatly that they would stay and ordered the airlift expanded to the full; by the time the blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949, some 2.32 million tons had come in by air. When North Korea invaded the South on 25 June 1950, the UN Security Council, with the Soviet Union absent, passed a resolution calling on member states to help, and Truman, without a declaration of war by Congress, decided to commit naval, air and ground forces, calling it a “police action” at a press conference on 29 June.

kin.name: Margaret Thatcher
kin.why: When Argentina invaded the Falklands on 2 April 1982, she won the backing of a UN condemnation and within days approved an operation to send a task force and retake the islands. On 14 June, 74 days later, the Argentine forces surrendered; 255 British and 649 Argentine servicemen had died.

kin.name: Julius Nyerere
kin.why: When Idi Amin of Uganda invaded the Kagera region of northwestern Tanzania in 1978 and declared it annexed, Nyerere struck back at once. Advancing alongside Ugandan exiles, his forces took the capital, Kampala, in April 1979, and Amin fled the country.

you: You saw that leaving a rule-breaker alone invites something worse next time, and you chose to respond without hesitation. But you want that response to be one that many nations endorse together, not force wielded alone. At your core is a refusal to push hard decisions onto others and a readiness to take them on yourself.
caution: A quick response easily skips over procedure. When Truman sent troops to Korea in June 1950 without the approval of Congress, Senator Taft argued that he had no legal authority to do so, and critics charged that it set a precedent for presidents to wage war without a declaration.

name: The Wałęsa
line: A reconciler who stands firm, waits, and wins through negotiation
story: Solidarity and the Round Table talks (1980–1989)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Alliance and Caution, this type does not bend on justice and principle, yet its goal is not to destroy the other side but to make both live together under the same rules. It builds pressure by widening its base of support at home and abroad, and it knows how to wait a long time, until the other side has no choice but to negotiate. Even after winning, it chooses reconciliation over revenge to steady the new order. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to what Kennedy said on the night of 24 October: keep up the blockade, but leave the other side a way out so that it is not seen to have capitulated completely.

figure.name: Lech Wałęsa
figure.life: Born on 29 September 1943 in Popowo, in German-occupied Poland, he went to work as an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk in 1967. He helped organize the shipyard protests of 1970 against rises in food prices; fired in 1976 for illegal union activity, he climbed over the shipyard wall on 14 August 1980 to lead a strike and became chairman of the independent trade union Solidarity, founded that year. Under martial law, declared on 13 December 1981, he was interned for 11 months, and in 1983 his wife, Danuta, accepted his Nobel Peace Prize for him because he feared he would not be let back in if he left the country. Elected president in December 1990, he served until 1995 but was criticized for his feuds with old comrades and his coarse language, and he lost his bid for reelection in 1995. Allegations that he collaborated with the secret police in the 1970s resurfaced with a book by historians in 2008 and a handwriting analysis by the Institute of National Remembrance in 2017; he denies them, and the dispute goes on.
figure.story: After leading the strike at the Gdańsk shipyard from 14 August 1980, Wałęsa concluded the Gdańsk Agreement with the government on 31 August, winning the right to strike and to form independent unions, and Solidarity grew into an organization of more than ten million members. Martial law in December 1981 banned the union, but when strikes broke out again in 1988, the government came to the table. At the Round Table talks, held from 6 February to 5 April 1989, the two sides agreed on partly free elections and a new Senate, and in the elections of 4 June Solidarity won 160 of the 161 contested seats in the Sejm, the lower house, and 99 of the 100 seats in the Senate. On 24 August that year Tadeusz Mazowiecki became prime minister, at the head of a government not led by the Communist Party.

kin.name: Nelson Mandela
kin.why: Sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964 and held for more than 27 years, he refused in 1985 an offer of release on condition that he renounce violence; freed in February 1990, he led the negotiations, and in 1994 he became president through the first election open to all races. In power, he set up the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, putting reconciliation ahead of punishment.

kin.name: Kim Dae-jung
kin.why: Persecuted again and again, kidnapped in Tokyo in August 1973 and sentenced to death in 1980, he was elected president in 1997, and on 15 June 2000 he held the first inter-Korean summit since the division, winning the Nobel Peace Prize that year. Critics say his record was tarnished by secret payments to North Korea and by his sons’ corruption.

you: You did not retreat on principle, yet you chose to draw the other side onto a path of living together rather than to break it. You are not impatient even when gathering supporters and building pressure takes a long time, and you think first about what order will remain after you win. For you, victory is closer to winning the other side’s consent than its surrender.
caution: Winning by holding to principle is one thing; steadying the new order afterward can be another. In 1990 Wałęsa split with his old Solidarity comrades and fought them in what was called the “war at the top,” and after governments changed every year of his presidency, he lost his bid for reelection in 1995.

name: The Sadat
line: A negotiator who walks into the heart of the enemy camp
story: The visit to Jerusalem and the Camp David Accords (1977–1978)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Independent and Speed, this type makes international law and legitimacy the basis of negotiation and believes that even a long-blocked situation can be unlocked by a deal. Rather than wait for the consent of allies or neighbors, it goes in person, alone if need be, into the other camp to settle matters face to face. When a chance to change the situation appears, it moves fast and accepts the risk. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to Khrushchev on 26 October, when, without convening the Presidium, he wrote the “knot” letter himself and proposed trading withdrawal for a pledge of no invasion.

figure.name: Anwar Sadat
figure.life: Born on 25 December 1918 in Mit Abu al-Kum in the Nile Delta, he graduated from the military academy in Cairo in 1938. He was jailed during the Second World War on suspicion of contacts with the Germans, and again in 1946 over the assassination of a pro-British politician. In the Free Officers’ revolution of July 1952 he read the first statement over the radio, and after serving as vice president he became president when Nasser died in 1970. Having sent the Soviet military advisers home in 1972, he attacked Israel by surprise together with Syria on 6 October 1973. In 1974 his open-door policy drew in foreign capital, but rising prices and corruption led to the bread riots of January 1977. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Begin in 1978, but was criticized for repressive rule, as when he arrested some 1,500 critics in a single sweep in September 1981, and on 6 October that year he was assassinated by Islamist officers at a victory parade.
figure.story: On 9 November 1977 Sadat told parliament that for the sake of peace he would go even to the Israeli parliament in Jerusalem. His foreign minister, Ismail Fahmy, objected and resigned, but on the night of 19 November Sadat landed at Tel Aviv airport, and on the 20th he addressed the Knesset. It was the first official visit to Israel by the head of an Arab state, and in December Syria, Iraq, Libya and others, meeting in Tripoli, Libya, condemned it. With US President Carter mediating, he signed the Camp David Accords with Prime Minister Begin on 17 September 1978, concluded a peace treaty in Washington on 26 March 1979, and by April 1982 had recovered the whole of the Sinai Peninsula.

kin.name: Willy Brandt
kin.why: Becoming chancellor in 1969, he pushed ahead with Ostpolitik, meeting the East German premier at Erfurt in March 1970 and concluding treaties with Moscow and Warsaw that year. Kneeling before the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising on 7 December was a decision he made knowing it would meet resistance: 48% of West Germans said it went too far.

kin.name: F. W. de Klerk
kin.why: Five months after becoming president in September 1989, he announced in a speech to parliament on 2 February 1990 that the African National Congress and other banned organizations would be legalized, and on 11 February he released Mandela. Against the opposition of his own supporters he ended apartheid through negotiation, and in 1993 he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Mandela.

you: You were convinced that a long-blocked problem is solved only when someone moves first, and you chose to take that first step yourself. Ready for opposition and misunderstanding around you, you aim to sit down directly with the other side and produce a result. Holding principle and bargaining together, you go into a negotiation with a clear line between what you can concede and what you must keep.
caution: Get too far ahead alone, and your supporters at home and your allies may not follow. Sadat’s separate peace treaty of 1979 left him watching Egypt suspended from the Arab League and the League’s headquarters move from Cairo to Tunis, and in October 1981 he died at the hands of his own officers, at a parade of his own army.

name: The Kekkonen
line: A diplomat of survival who lives in the shadow of a great power
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Independent and Caution, this type believes that even from a position of weakness it can win a seat at the table by invoking treaties and neutrality. It never fully enters either camp, trades in trust with its powerful neighbor, and waits without hurry for the other side’s circumstances to change. A realist, it does not shrink from braving criticism at home or abandoning yesterday’s position if that is what it takes to secure its country’s survival. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to Macmillan, who backed the American blockade but, in a telephone call on 26 October, offered to immobilize Britain’s Thor missiles, and so made a place for his country in the bargaining.

figure.name: Urho Kekkonen
figure.life: Born on 3 September 1900 in Pielavesi in central Finland, he fought with the Whites in the civil war of 1918 and earned a doctorate in law in 1936. He joined the Agrarian League in 1933, served as minister of justice and of the interior, and was twice prime minister in the 1950s. Elected president in 1956 by an electoral college vote of 151 to 149, he made trust with the Soviet Union the axis of his foreign policy: in January 1959 he went to Moscow and resolved the “Night Frost” crisis of 1958, in which Soviet economic pressure had brought down the cabinet, and in 1975 he presided over the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in Helsinki. But a special law extended his term by four years in 1973, the conservative opposition was kept out of government for nearly twenty years, and he used relations with Moscow to keep his rivals down; for all this he drew criticism as an authoritarian and the jibe of “Finlandization.” Failing health forced him to step down on 26 October 1981, and he died in Helsinki on 31 August 1986.
figure.story: On 30 October 1961 the Soviet Union sent Finland a note proposing military consultations under the 1948 friendship treaty against the threat of a NATO attack. To agree would undermine neutrality; to refuse would breach the treaty. Kekkonen dissolved parliament on 14 November to bring the general election forward, and on 24 November he spent a full day in talks with Khrushchev in Novosibirsk. Saying he trusted Kekkonen, Khrushchev agreed to put off the consultations indefinitely, and on the 26th Kekkonen announced it in a broadcast. His rival candidate, Honka, had withdrawn on the 25th, and in 1962 Kekkonen was reelected with 199 of the 300 electoral votes. How far Kekkonen himself engineered the crisis is still debated.

kin.name: Gwanghaegun
kin.why: After taking the throne in 1608, he chose a course that bound him to neither the declining Ming nor the rising Later Jin. When the Ming demanded troops in 1619, he sent Gang Hong-rip with more than 13,000 men but told him to move as circumstances dictated, and Gang, defeated, surrendered to the Later Jin. This neutral diplomacy became one of the justifications for the coup that put King Injo on the throne in 1623.

kin.name: Bruno Kreisky
kin.why: As Austria’s chancellor from 1970 to 1983, he made permanent neutrality the basis of an active foreign policy. He offered Vienna as a meeting ground for East and West, and there Carter and Brezhnev signed SALT II on 18 June 1979; in 1980 he gave the PLO unofficial recognition. He was criticized for appointing ministers with Nazi pasts.

you: When strength was lacking, you chose to win a place at the table by invoking rules and legitimacy. Rather than stay long on one side, you watch how things develop and pick the path of least loss, aiming above all for your country’s survival. Changing position along the way does not trouble you much.
caution: Flexibility for the sake of survival can bend even the rules at home. In January 1973 Kekkonen had parliament extend his term by four years through a special law, and because he kept the opposition out of power for so long on the grounds that Moscow distrusted it, Finland came to look back on his era, after he had gone, with the word “Finlandization.”

name: The Bush
line: A negotiator who binds a coalition together to build a way out
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Alliance and Speed, this type judges quickly when crisis strikes, but it seeks legitimacy for its actions not in its own strength alone but in the resolutions of international organizations and the participation of allies. It binds allies together one by one through phone calls and meetings, and it raises the pressure by arranging deals that share out the fighting and the costs. It sets its goal narrowly in advance and goes no further once the goal is reached. Measured against October 1962, it is Kennedy’s own decision: keep up the blockade, and on the evening of 27 October answer Khrushchev’s letter of 26 October by trading withdrawal for a pledge of no invasion.

figure.name: George H. W. Bush
figure.life: Born in Milton, Massachusetts, on 12 June 1924, he joined the Navy on his 18th birthday; shot down during a raid on Chichi-jima in the Pacific in 1944, he was rescued and received the Distinguished Flying Cross. After graduating from Yale in 1948 he went into the oil business in Texas, then served as a congressman, ambassador to the UN, head of the liaison office in Beijing and director of Central Intelligence before spending eight years as Reagan’s vice president from 1981. Becoming president in 1989, he invaded Panama that December and met Gorbachev at Malta; he supported German unification in 1990, and after the Gulf War his approval rating reached 89% in March 1991. But he broke his 1988 campaign promise not to raise taxes with the budget deal of 1990, and amid recession he lost to Clinton in 1992. Some praise the prudence of his diplomacy; others fault him for neglecting problems at home. He died in Houston on 30 November 2018.
figure.story: When Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, the UN Security Council condemned the invasion that same day, and on 7 August Bush ordered Operation Desert Shield, sending troops to Saudi Arabia. Gathering the support of the Council, the Soviet Union included, he won passage on 29 November of a resolution authorizing force if Iraq did not withdraw by 15 January 1991, and while drawing more than 30 nations into the coalition he had most of the cost of the war borne by Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Germany, Japan and others. The air campaign began on 17 January 1991 and the ground war on 24 February, and once Kuwait was liberated the attack was halted on 28 February. Not marching on Baghdad was a decision to stay within the bounds of the resolution.

kin.name: Helmut Kohl
kin.why: When the Berlin Wall opened in November 1989, he put forward a step-by-step plan for unification within weeks, and in July 1990 he won Gorbachev’s consent for a united Germany to remain in NATO. In September the two German states and the four victorious powers concluded the “Two Plus Four” treaty, and unification followed on 3 October. He finished the work within a year, inside the framework of alliances and treaties.

kin.name: Roh Tae-woo
kin.why: After launching his Nordpolitik officially with the declaration of 7 July 1988, he established relations with Hungary in 1989 and with the Soviet Union on 30 September 1990. The two Koreas’ simultaneous entry into the UN in September 1991, the inter-Korean Basic Agreement that December, and relations with China in August 1992 were all achieved within five years, on the foundation of the alliance with the United States.

you: When crisis struck, you chose to look for a path that neither retreats nor charges in blindly. You aim to raise the pressure while also holding out an exit the other side can accept, and along the way you treat the support of allies as a precious asset. You are used to hearing many views in a short time and then making the call.
caution: Stop at the goal the coalition agreed on, and you may be unable to answer for what lies outside it. On 15 February 1991 Bush called on the Iraqi military and people to force Saddam Hussein aside, yet when the Shia and the Kurds rose up in March he did not intervene; the uprisings were crushed by early April, and tens of thousands died.

name: The Acheson
line: A designer who builds order through treaties and institutions
story: Designing the Marshall Plan and NATO (1947–1949)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Alliance and Caution, this type believes order can be kept through treaties and institutions rather than war, and works hard to build frameworks that many states uphold together. It contains the other side without colliding with it head-on, and it strikes bargains with allies, giving aid and security guarantees in return for shared obligations. It designs structures meant to last rather than playing for a single decisive result. Measured against October 1962, it comes closest to the role of the UN, which tried to bring both sides to one table through Security Council meetings and the secretary-general’s letters, and to the path that led to the hotline and the Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963.

figure.name: Dean Acheson
figure.life: Born in Middletown, Connecticut, on 11 April 1893, he graduated from Yale and Harvard Law School and clerked for Supreme Court Justice Brandeis. He became under secretary of the Treasury in 1933 but resigned in opposition to Roosevelt’s gold policy; he returned to government at the State Department in 1941 and was under secretary of state from 1945 to 1947. In 1947 he drafted the Truman Doctrine speech requesting aid for Greece and Turkey, and he served as secretary of state from January 1949 to January 1953. Throughout his tenure he faced charges that his speech of January 1950 had left Korea outside the defense perimeter, and McCarthy’s attacks over the “loss of China.” During the Cuban crisis of 1962, among Kennedy’s advisers, he opposed the decision to stop at a blockade, and in 1968 he advised Johnson to get out of Vietnam quickly. He won the Pulitzer Prize in 1970 for his memoirs and died at his farm in Maryland on 12 October 1971.
figure.story: In May 1947, as under secretary of state, Acheson said publicly for the first time, in a speech to the Delta Council in Cleveland, Mississippi, that Europe needed large-scale aid, and on 5 June Secretary of State Marshall took up the idea in a speech at Harvard. That July sixteen European nations met in Paris to draw up a joint recovery plan, and on 3 April 1948 Truman signed the aid act. As secretary of state, Acheson concluded the negotiations for the North Atlantic Treaty that had begun in secret talks in March 1948, and on 4 April 1949 in Washington he signed it together with the foreign ministers of the twelve founding nations, among them Canada, Britain and France. Because Truman declined to sign, it is Acheson’s name that stands on the treaty, which came into force on 24 August that year.

kin.name: Robert Schuman
kin.why: As French foreign minister (1948–1952), on 9 May 1950 he issued a declaration proposing that French and West German coal and steel production be placed under a common authority. The European Coal and Steel Community, founded by six nations, was designed to prevent war by managing the raw materials of war in common, and from 1958 to 1960 he was the first president of the forerunner of the European Parliament.

kin.name: Yoshida Shigeru
kin.why: Prime minister in 1946–1947 and 1948–1954, he signed the San Francisco Peace Treaty and the US–Japan Security Treaty on 8 September 1951. His course of leaving security to the United States and concentrating on the economy later came to be called the “Yoshida Doctrine”; some criticize it for giving up diplomatic autonomy, others credit it with opening the way to postwar prosperity.

you: You valued rules that endure over a single victory. You do not find it tiresome to bring states with differing interests together to find common ground, and you aim for predictable stability over sudden change. Your calculation is to secure, within that order, a respected place for your country.
caution: Those who design an order tend to draw a line around its outside. In a speech on 12 January 1950 Acheson left Korea out of America’s defense perimeter, and when the Korean War broke out five months later he was accused for the rest of his life of having invited it. Research in Soviet documents suggests the speech had little effect.
